extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and policymakers interested in civil liberties and free speech
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical principles and practical limits for individual liberty—especially freedom of thought, speech, association, and the conditions under which society or government may legitimately restrict them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inward domain of consciousness (liberty of conscience, thought, and feeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberty comprises the inward domain of consciousness: liberty of conscience in the most comprehensive sense; liberty of thought and feeling; absolute freedom of opinion and sentiment on all subjects, practical or speculative, scientific, moral, or theological.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expression and publishing of opinions are practically inseparable from liberty of thought because they rest largely on the same reasons. Protecting the internal sphere of belief is foundational to other liberties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of expression and publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom to express and publish opinions is essential and almost inseparable from liberty of thought, even though it concerns conduct affecting others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when expression affects others, its protection is justified by its nearly equal importance to thought itself. Restrictions should be treated cautiously and only when other exacting conditions (see restrictions criteria) are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of tastes and pursuits (personal lifestyle freedom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberty includes freedom of tastes and pursuits: framing the plan of our life to suit our own character; doing as we like, subject to consequences, without impediment by fellow-creatures so long as what we do does not harm them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Society should permit individuals to live as they choose even if others deem their conduct foolish or wrong, provided no harm to others results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of combination (freedom of association)
rubrics_metrics.description: From individual liberty follows liberty to combine: freedom to unite for any purpose not involving harm to others, with participants being of full age and not forced or deceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associational freedom is protected so long as membership is voluntary and the group's purposes do not harm others; coercion, deception, or involvement of minors undermines legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm principle — the only justifiable limit on liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: The only freedom deserving the name is pursuing our own good in our own way, so long as we do not attempt to deprive others of theirs, or impede their efforts to obtain it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a general rule for judging when society may legitimately interfere: interference is justified only to prevent direct harm to others, not simply because conduct is foolish, immoral, or offensive to prevailing opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illegitimacy of social or majoritarian coercion of opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: No right exists for the people (or a government acting as their organ) to coerce opinions; the power is illegitimate even when exercised by a majority or by a government aligned with public sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Majority agreement does not justify silencing minorities; 'all mankind minus one' being of one opinion does not make silencing the one permissible. Anti-pattern: using popular belief as sole justification for suppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silencing opinions robs humanity and posterity
rubrics_metrics.description: Silencing an opinion is robbing the human race and posterity: if the opinion is true, people lose the opportunity to exchange error for truth; if wrong, they lose the clearer perception of truth produced by its collision with error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even suppression of apparently false opinions harms public reason and future understanding. Policy makers should weigh long-term epistemic loss when considering restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silencing assumes infallibility and is therefore unjustifiable
rubrics_metrics.description: Refusing a hearing to an opinion because we are 'sure' it is false is to assume that our certainty equals absolute certainty; all silencing of discussion is an assumption of infallibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because individuals and institutions are fallible, forbidding discussion on grounds of perceived falsity illegitimately claims absolute certainty. Anti-pattern: treating provisional certainty as justification for censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions only where speech is linked to overt wrongful acts (incitement standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instigation to wrongful acts (example: incitement to tyrannicide) may be a proper subject of punishment only if an overt act has followed and a probable connection can be established between the instigation and the act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets a high threshold for punishing speech: mere advocacy or expression—even of immoral doctrines—does not justify punishment absent a probable causal link to imminent harmful action. Example given: discussion of tyrannicide might be punishable only with overt act and probable connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of free discussion for correction of error and attainment of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Human errors are corrigible; the capacity to rectify mistakes depends on discussion and experience. Facts generally do not 'tell their own story' without commentary; discussion is required to interpret experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keeping means of correction (open debate, criticism) constantly at hand is essential for reliable judgment. Anti-pattern: insulating beliefs from criticism undermines their justification and the public's approach to truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom to contradict and disprove as condition for assuming truth for action
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete liberty of contradicting and disproving an opinion is the very condition which justifies assuming it true for purposes of action; without liberty to contest, assuming truth is unjustified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities or individuals may act on beliefs only after those beliefs have been exposed to open challenge; otherwise, acting as if belief is certain is illegitimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility is not an independent ground for restricting discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: The usefulness of an opinion is itself a matter of opinion and requires discussion; therefore one cannot legitimately prohibit discussion on the ground that an opinion is useful to society without allowing defenders to contest its truth or utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: restricting dissent on 'usefulness' grounds while allowing defenders of orthodoxy to deploy both truth and utility arguments. If a doctrine's usefulness is at stake, it must be open to the same debate as its truth.
